marrow__ANAT_CH24_Q001.takeaway: The red nucleus is a superior-colliculus-level midbrain nucleus.
marrow__ANAT_CH24_Q001.displayText: The red nucleus lies in the midbrain at the level of the superior colliculus. At the inferior-colliculus level the nuclei include inferior colliculus, substantia nigra, trochlear nucleus, and mesencephalic nucleus of V; at superior-colliculus level they include superior colliculus, substantia nigra, trochlear and oculomotor nuclei, Edinger–Westphal nucleus, mesencephalic nucleus of V, and red nucleus. Both levels contain the cerebral aqueduct. Descending motor tracts include corticospinal and corticonuclear fibers, temporopontine/frontopontine fibers and medial longitudinal fasciculus; the superior level additionally shows rubrospinal decussation. Sensory structures differ by level: inferior level includes lateral, trigeminal spinal, and medial lemnisci and superior cerebellar peduncle decussation; superior level includes trigeminal spinal and medial lemnisci.

rationales.b: Inferior colliculus marks the auditory midbrain level; red nucleus is listed at the superior-colliculus level.
rationales.c: The pons is caudal to midbrain and does not contain the red nucleus.
rationales.d: The medulla is below the pons and has no red nucleus.

marrow__ANAT_CH24_Q002.takeaway: Weber syndrome combines ipsilateral oculomotor palsy and contralateral hemiplegia; tectum is behind the aqueduct.
marrow__ANAT_CH24_Q002.displayText: The clinical combination of contralateral hemiplegia and third-nerve paralysis suggests Weber syndrome in the midbrain. The tectum lies posterior to the cerebral aqueduct. The superior colliculi mediate visual reflexes; their brachium connects to lateral geniculate body and optic tract. The inferior colliculi are auditory centers and their brachium connects to medial geniculate body. The trochlear nerve emerges in the midline below the inferior colliculi. Internally, substantia nigra separates crus cerebri from tegmentum; tectum is dorsal/posterior to the aqueduct.
emphasis: tectum lies posterior to the cerebral aqueduct

rationales.a: Superior brachium links superior colliculus with lateral geniculate body and optic tract, not medial geniculate.
rationales.b: Trochlear nerve exits below the inferior colliculus, not above it.
rationales.c: Substantia nigra separates crus cerebri and tegmentum; tectum lies posterior to the aqueduct.

reconstruction.sourceFragment:
The given clinical scenario of contralateral hemiplegia and paralysis of the third cranial nerve is
suggestive of Weber syndrome involving the midbrain. In this, the tectum lies posterior to the
cerebral aqueduct.
The midbrain connects the pons and cerebellum with the forebrain. Externally, on the posterior
surface, there are two pairs of colliculi—the corpora quadrigemina:
+ The superior colliculi are centers for visual reflexes. The superior brachium connects the
superior colliculi to the lateral geniculate body and the optic tract.
+ The inferior colliculi are auditory centres, and the inferior brachium connects the inferior
colliculus to the medial geniculate body.

The trochlear nerve emerges in the midline below the inferior colliculi.
Internally, the midbrain comprises two cerebral peduncles. Each one is divided into an anterior
crus cerebri and a posterior tegmentum by the substantia nigra. The oculomotor nerve emerges
from a groove on the medial side of crus cerebri and passes to the lateral wall of the cavernous
sinus.

marrow__ANAT_CH24_Q003.takeaway: Lateral lemniscus is an auditory tract ending at inferior colliculus, absent at superior-colliculus level.
marrow__ANAT_CH24_Q003.displayText: Lateral lemniscus is not seen at the superior-colliculus level and therefore is not likely to be injured there. It is part of the auditory pathway and terminates at the inferior-colliculus level. The superior-colliculus section contains medial, spinal and trigeminal lemnisci, in addition to nuclei and motor tracts described for that level.
emphasis: not seen at the superior-colliculus level

rationales.a: Medial lemniscus is present at superior-colliculus level and conveys dorsal-column sensory information.
rationales.b: Spinal lemniscus is also present at the superior-colliculus section.
rationales.c: Trigeminal lemniscus is present at this level; lateral lemniscus is the auditory tract ending lower at inferior colliculus.

marrow__ANAT_CH24_Q004.takeaway: The rubrospinal tract crosses in the ventral tegmental decussation.
marrow__ANAT_CH24_Q004.displayText: The ventral tegmental decussation is formed by rubrospinal fibers. The red nucleus receives corticorubral fibers from cortex and cerebellorubral fibers from cerebellum, then sends rubrospinal efferents that cross at the superior-colliculus level and descend to spinal cord. The midbrain has four major decussations: at superior-colliculus level, ventral tegmental decussation of rubrospinal tract and dorsal tegmental decussation of tectospinal tract; at inferior-colliculus level, superior cerebellar peduncle decussation and trochlear nerve decussation.

rationales.a: Tectospinal fibers cross in the dorsal tegmental decussation, not the ventral one.
rationales.b: Tectobulbar fibers are not the tract named for the ventral tegmental decussation.
rationales.c: Vestibulospinal fibers descend uncrossed from vestibular nuclei; rubrospinal fibers cross ventrally.

reconstruction.sourceFragment:
The ventral tegmental decussation in the midbrain is due to the rubrospinal tract.
The red nucleus is situated at the level of superior colliculus.
+ It receives afferents from the corticorubral fibers in the cortex and the cerebellorubral fibers in
the cerebellum.
+ It sends out efferent fibers as the rubrospinal tract.
+ It decussates as ventral tegmental decussation at the level of the superior colliculus and descends
to the spinal cord.
The midbrain has four decussations:
+ At the level of the superior colliculus

+ Ventral tegmental decussation of the rubrospinal tract
+ Dorsal tegmental decussation of the tectospinal tract
+ At the level of the inferior colliculus
+ Decussation of superior cerebellar peduncles
+ Decussation of trochlear nerve

marrow__ANAT_CH24_Q005.takeaway: Frontopontine fibers occupy the medial crus cerebri.
marrow__ANAT_CH24_Q005.displayText: The most medial part of the crus cerebri carries frontopontine fibers. The middle two-thirds carry corticospinal and corticonuclear fibers; the lateral part carries temporopontine fibers.
emphasis: most medial part of the crus cerebri

rationales.a: Corticospinal and corticonuclear fibers occupy the middle two-thirds of crus cerebri.
rationales.c: Temporopontine fibers occupy the lateral crus, opposite the medial location asked.
rationales.d: Corticonuclear fibers lie in the middle two-thirds with corticospinal fibers, not alone in the most medial portion.

marrow__ANAT_CH24_Q006.takeaway: Substantia nigra degeneration is associated with paralysis agitans.
marrow__ANAT_CH24_Q006.displayText: The marked coronal midbrain structure is substantia nigra. The associated movement disorder is paralysis agitans (parkinsonism).

rationales.b: Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease is a prion encephalopathy, not the movement disorder tied to substantia nigra in this item.
rationales.c: Multiple system atrophy is a distinct neurodegenerative syndrome, not the keyed diagnosis.
rationales.d: Huntington disease causes chorea from striatal degeneration, unlike the source-associated parkinsonism.

marrow__ANAT_CH24_Q007.takeaway: Interpeduncular fossa contains tuber cinereum, infundibulum, mammillary bodies and oculomotor nerve, but not ophthalmic nerve.
marrow__ANAT_CH24_Q007.displayText: The ophthalmic nerve is not a content of the interpeduncular fossa. From anterior to posterior, the floor contains tuber cinereum, infundibular stalk, mammillary bodies, and posterior perforated substance, which is pierced by posterior cerebral arteries. The oculomotor nerve emerges between the superior cerebellar and posterior cerebral arteries in this fossa.
emphasis: not a content of the interpeduncular fossa

rationales.a: Mammillary bodies form the floor of the fossa and are explicitly listed as contents.
rationales.b: Tuber cinereum lies at the anterior floor and is listed as a content.
rationales.c: Oculomotor nerve emerges into the fossa between posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries.
